nameStory: The Atlantic brief squid gets its name from its remarkably short lifespan - these little cephalopods live fast and die young, typically surviving only a few months. The word 'brief' perfectly captures their fleeting existence, while 'Atlantic' tells us where to find them in the western waters of this ocean.
description: The Atlantic brief squid is a small, torpedo-shaped marine animal with eight arms and two longer tentacles, belonging to the same group as octopuses and cuttlefish. These diminutive squids typically grow to just a few inches long, making them one of the smaller squid species you might encounter. Their translucent, pale body can rapidly change color from clear to mottled brown or reddish hues. Like all squids, they're active predators that jet through the water by forcefully expelling water from their bodies.

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Noticeably tiny compared to other squids, fitting easily in your palm with a soft, gelatinous texture when handled

idTips.label: Color changing ability
idTips.description: Body rapidly shifts from nearly transparent to mottled browns and reds, creating a flickering, shimmering effect

idTips.label: Torpedo body shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, bullet-like body that feels smooth and slippery, with triangular fins at the rear end

idTips.label: Eight arms plus two tentacles
idTips.description: Eight shorter arms around the mouth plus two longer tentacles that can shoot out to grab prey, all covered in tiny suction cups

idTips.label: Large eyes
idTips.description: Prominent, dark eyes that seem oversized for the body, giving them an alert, almost curious appearance

habitat: Atlantic brief squids prefer shallow coastal waters along New England's shores, typically found in bays, harbors, and nearshore areas with sandy or muddy bottoms. They favor warmer waters and are more commonly spotted in the southern parts of New England, often around eelgrass beds and other underwater vegetation where small fish and crustaceans gather.

seasonality.spring: Brief squids begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, often found near the surface during calm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings, when they're most active in shallow bays and may be spotted from docks or while snorkeling in clear water.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less common as waters begin to cool, often moving to slightly deeper areas or migrating south.
seasonality.winter: Rare to absent in New England waters as they cannot tolerate cold temperatures and either die off or move to warmer southern waters.

funFact: Atlantic brief squids are essentially the mayflies of the sea - their entire adult life cycle lasts only about 3-4 months, during which they must grow, find a mate, reproduce, and die, making every encounter with one a glimpse of an animal living life in extreme fast-forward.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young longfin squids, but brief squids are much smaller and have proportionally larger eyes relative to their body size. Remember: if it fits comfortably in your hand and has huge, prominent eyes, it's probably a brief squid.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'brief squids,' they're not actually closely related to the common market squid you might eat - they belong to a different genus entirely and are much too small for commercial harvesting.
compareHints: As the only Lolliguncula species in New England waters, brief squids are most similar to longfin squids in the same family, but are significantly smaller and have a shorter lifespan. Unlike their longfin cousins which can live over a year and grow much larger, brief squids pack their entire existence into just a few months and rarely exceed a few inches in length.
